# Tabs

Several panels, one shown at a time, chosen from a row of tabs.

```tsx
import { Tabs } from "@rata/react";
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `tabs` |
| Family | navigation |
| Tier | free |
| Status (css / react / figma) | latest / latest / future |
| Depends on | `state-layer`, `icon` |

## Behavior

A `tablist` of `tab` buttons over a set of `tabpanel` regions, with roving tabindex and arrow-key movement along the declared axis. Every tab points at its panel and every panel back at its tab, which is the pairing that makes a tablist a tablist.

Headless contract: `getTabsProps` in `packages/primitives/src/tabs.ts` — importable from `@rata/primitives` without the React wrapper or any CSS.

- **Which of three, when they all look like one bar of options** — Three components here can look like one enclosed bar of options, so each one's contract says which is which. SegmentedControl is a question with a short fixed set of answers: single, always filled, cannot be cleared. ToggleButtonGroup is the same ARIA pattern with a wider API — multiple selection, deselection, vertical orientation, the toggle-button variants — so reach for it when you need any of those. Tabs is a different pattern entirely: tabs reveal a region, each naming a panel and each panel naming its tab, and if what is being chosen is which content is shown rather than what gets submitted, it is Tabs — which can be drawn to look exactly like the other two and is still announced as a tablist.
- **It is not a segmented control, and no longer looks like one either** — `SegmentedControl` is the component for that, and the two are not the same control however they are painted. A segmented control picks a VALUE: it is a radiogroup, every option is announced as a choice, and the answer is submitted with the rest of the form. Tabs reveal a REGION: moving between them changes what is on screen rather than what will be sent. Using one for the other is not a style error — a radiogroup standing in for tabs tells a screen reader a form is being filled in, and tabs standing in for a form control hide the answer inside a region nobody submits.

Tabs carried a segmented appearance for a while, added when that look had nothing of its own. Once it did, two components able to draw the same bar made the pair harder to tell apart in precisely the place the difference matters — so the appearance went with it. Tabs look like tabs.
- **Activation is the caller's choice, because it has a cost** — Automatic — the arrow keys select as they move — is what APG recommends and what a reader expects, but arrowing past four tabs then renders four panels. Manual moves focus and waits for Enter or Space, which is right when a panel fetches something. The wrong one is not cosmetic: automatic over an expensive panel fires requests nobody asked for.
- **An items array rather than children** — The component owns the id wiring that makes a tablist a tablist — every tab pointing at its panel, every panel back at its tab — and that is the error-prone part. Handing it out to be assembled would mean cloning elements to inject ids, and a mis-wired pair looks perfectly fine on screen. The trade is that a tab is a label and some content rather than arbitrary structure; if that stops being enough the API should change rather than the caller working around it.
- **Every panel stays mounted, all but one hidden** — Unmounting would throw away whatever state each panel held — a half-filled form, a scroll position, an expanded row — every time the reader glanced at another tab. `hidden` keeps them out of the accessibility tree and out of the tab order without destroying them.
- **A panel is in the tab order even with nothing focusable inside it** — Without `tabIndex={0}` on the panel, Tab from the tablist skips a panel of plain text entirely and the reader never reaches the content the tab just promised them.
- **A horizontal strip scrolls; it never wraps** — A tab keeps its label on one line, so a strip with more tabs than its column is wide has to give somewhere. It scrolls sideways, the same bargain TopNav's list makes and for the same reason: a strip that grows to a second row moves everything below it, and a wrapped row of tabs reads as a mistake rather than as a choice. Before this it did neither and simply overflowed, which on a narrow viewport took the whole page into horizontal scroll — one strip of six families dragging every column of prose beside it.

Two details are load-bearing. The rule the markers sit on is drawn on the scrolling element itself, so it stays put while the tabs move under it. And the list carries bottom padding of exactly the rule's width, because the selected tab's marker hangs below its tab to cover that rule and a scroll container clips whatever hangs outside it — without the padding the marker loses its bottom half the moment a strip becomes scrollable. The cost is that the marker now sits flush on the rule rather than over it, which is one device pixel.

The scrollbar is hidden. This is a row of controls rather than a region to explore, every tab is reachable with the arrow keys regardless of what is on screen, and the marker under the selected tab already says there is more than one.

## Props

Extends `Omit<HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>, "children">`.

| Prop | Type | Default | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `TabItem[]` | — | The tabs and their panels, in the order they are read. |
| `value?` | `string` | — | Which panel is showing. Makes the component controlled. |
| `defaultValue?` | `string` | — | Starting panel for uncontrolled tabs. Defaults to the first. |
| `onValueChange?` | `(value: string) => void` | — | Called with the panel that should be shown. |
| `label?` | `string` | — | Accessible name for the tablist. |
| `labelledBy?` | `string` | — | Names the tablist from an element the reader can see. |
| `orientation?` | `TabsOrientation` | `"horizontal"` | Which axis the tabs run along. |
| `activation?` | `TabsActivation` | `"automatic"` | Whether the arrow keys select as they move. |
| `className?` | `string` | — | Extra classes on the wrapper, for placement — not for restyling it. |

### `items`

```ts
items: TabItem[]
```

The tabs and their panels, in the order they are read.

**Use when**

- Two to about six panels of one thing seen different ways: an invoice's details, its history, its notes.

**Don't use for**

- Steps in a sequence. Tabs are peers a reader moves between freely; a process with an order and a completion state is not this.
- One tab. A tablist of one is a heading with extra keyboard behaviour.
- Navigation between pages. These are regions of one page — a destination belongs in a nav, where it has an address.

**Accessibility** Each entry becomes a `tab` pointing at its `tabpanel` with `aria-controls`, and the panel points back with `aria-labelledby`. The selected tab carries `aria-selected`; the rest are `hidden`, which keeps them out of both the accessibility tree and the tab order.

### `value`

```ts
value?: string
```

Which panel is showing. Makes the component controlled.

**Use when**

- Driving the selection from a URL, so a tab can be linked to and survives a reload.

**Don't use for**

- Passing it alongside `defaultValue`.

**Conflicts with** `defaultValue`

### `defaultValue`

```ts
defaultValue?: string
```

Starting panel for uncontrolled tabs. Defaults to the first.

**Use when**

- Opening on something other than the first panel.

**Conflicts with** `value`

### `onValueChange`

```ts
onValueChange?: (value: string) => void
```

Called with the panel that should be shown.

**Use when**

- Controlled mode, to set `value`.
- Loading a panel's data the first time it is opened.

**Don't use for**

- Assuming it fires once per tab. Under automatic activation it fires for every tab the arrow keys pass through — which is the reason `activation` exists.

### `label`

```ts
label?: string
```

Accessible name for the tablist.

Source doc: Accessible name for the tablist. Required unless `labelledBy` names an element.

**Use when**

- Naming what the tabs divide: "Invoice" for a set covering one invoice's details, history and notes.

**Don't use for**

- The word "tabs", which the role already says.

**Accessibility** Becomes the tablist's `aria-label`. Required unless `labelledBy` names an element — a tablist with no name is announced as a bare tablist.

### `labelledBy`

```ts
labelledBy?: string
```

Names the tablist from an element the reader can see.

**Use when**

- Pointing at the heading the tabs sit under, so the name changes with it.

**Don't use for**

- Passing it alongside `label` and expecting both. This one wins, and never renders the other.

**Accessibility** Wins over `label`, because it points at text on screen.

### `orientation`

```ts
orientation?: TabsOrientation = "horizontal"
```

Which axis the tabs run along.

**Use when**

- `vertical` for a long set, or beside a wide panel.

**Don't use for**

- `vertical` for two or three short tabs, where a row is easier to scan.

**Accessibility** Announced as `aria-orientation`, and it decides which arrow keys move: left/right on the horizontal axis, up/down on the vertical. Announcing it is a promise the component keeps.

### `activation`

```ts
activation?: TabsActivation = "automatic"
```

Whether the arrow keys select as they move.

**Use when**

- `automatic` — the default, and what a reader expects — when the panels are already on the client.
- `manual` when opening a panel costs something: a request, a render nobody asked for.

**Don't use for**

- `automatic` over panels that fetch. Arrowing across four tabs fires four requests, and the reader wanted the fifth.

**Accessibility** Both are conforming. `manual` moves focus and waits for Enter or Space; `automatic` selects as focus moves. A disabled tab is reachable either way — this system's disabled controls stay focusable — and selection does not follow focus onto it.

### `className`

```ts
className?: string
```

Extra classes on the wrapper, for placement — not for restyling it.

**Use when**

- Constraining the width, or spacing the set from what surrounds it.

**Don't use for**

- Making it look like a segmented control. They are different patterns, and the appearance is the only cue a sighted reader gets — which is why this component stopped offering that appearance itself.

## Use cases

### One thing seen several ways

The commonest case: panels of the same subject, all already loaded.

```tsx
<Tabs
  label="Invoice"
  items={[
    { value: "details", label: "Details", content: <Details /> },
    { value: "history", label: "History", content: <History /> },
    { value: "notes", label: "Notes", content: <Notes /> },
  ]}
/>
```

Automatic activation, which is the default: the panels are on the client, so selecting as the arrows move costs nothing and is what a reader expects.

### Panels that cost something to open

A panel fetches, so arrowing past it must not.

```tsx
<Tabs
  label="Invoice"
  activation="manual"
  value={tab}
  onValueChange={(next) => {
    setTab(next);
    load(next);
  }}
  items={items}
/>
```

`manual` is the whole point here: under automatic, arrowing from the first tab to the fourth fires three requests for panels nobody wanted to see. Controlled as well, so the tab can come from the URL and survive a reload.

### Don't: tabs standing in for a segmented control

Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.

```tsx
{/* Don't: this is a choice being made, not a region being revealed. */}
<Tabs
  label="Billing period"
  items={[
    { value: "monthly", label: "Monthly", content: null },
    { value: "annual", label: "Annual", content: null },
  ]}
/>
```

Don't. Empty panels are the tell: nothing is being revealed, so this is a question being answered — `SegmentedControl`, which is what that component is for. Tabs tell a screen reader that regions are being shown and hidden, and the answer here would sit inside a region nobody submits.

## Real usage in this repo

```tsx
<Tabs
        label="Invoice"
        items={[
          { value: "details", label: "Details", content: "Amount, dates, and the client." },
          { value: "history", label: "History", content: "Every change, most recent first." },
          { value: "notes", label: "Notes", content: "Anything the team wrote down." },
        ]}
      />
```

## Token recipe

### base

The set. Tabs read as an edge with a marker on it, and only that — there was a segmented appearance for a while, added when that look had no component of its own. SegmentedControl is that component now, and two things able to draw the same bar made the pair hard to tell apart in exactly the place the difference matters.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| rule under the tabs | `border.default solid theme.border.default` |
| gap between tabs | `space.gap.xs` |
| gap between the list and the panel | `space.padding.md` |
| gap between a vertical list and its panel | `space.gap.lg` |

### tab

One tab. The resting tone is the secondary text colour, so the selected one reads as emphasised rather than the rest reading as dimmed.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| colour | `theme.fg.secondary` |
| block-size | `size.control.md` |
| padding-inline | `space.control.padding-inline.sm` |
| border-radius | `radius.element` |
| font-size | `type.control.size.sm` |
| font-weight | `type.control.weight` |
| gap between icon and label | `space.gap.sm` |
| icon size | `size.icon.text` |
| hover / press | `compose the .rata-state-layer class` |
| focus ring | `theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible` |
| disabled | `state.disabled-opacity` |

### tab-selected

The panel you are looking at. Marked twice over: the bar is the visual cue and aria-selected is the announced one, so the state is never carried by colour alone.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| colour | `theme.fg.primary` |
| indicator | `theme.accent-role.bg at border.2, straddling the list's rule so the tab reads as joined to its panel` |

### panel

The region a tab reveals. Focusable even with nothing focusable inside, so Tab from the tablist reaches it.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| padding-block-start | `space.padding.md` |
| focus ring | `theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible` |
